meta.drug: extended-release niacin 2 g + laropiprant 40 mg daily (Tredaptive/Cordaptive, MK-0524A) added to simvastatin 40 mg +/- ezetimibe 10 mg
meta.sponsor: University of Oxford CTSU (regulatory sponsor), funded by Merck
meta.mechanism: Nicotinic acid (HCAR2/GPR109A/HM74A agonist) combined with laropiprant (PTGDR/DP1 prostaglandin D2 receptor antagonist, added only to reduce flushing). Target attribution for niacin is ambiguous: HCAR2 mediates anti-lipolysis and flushing, but the lipid effects (HDL-C up; LDL-C, apoB, TG, Lp(a) down) appear largely HCAR2-independent (Lauring et al. 2012: lipid efficacy preserved in GPR109A-knockout mice; full GPR109A agonists failed in humans). Proposed alternative mechanisms include hepatic DGAT2 inhibition, reduced VLDL/apoB and apo(a) production. Trial tested HDL-raising / multi-lipid modification on top of effective statin therapy.
meta.indication: secondary prevention of major vascular events in patients with prior MI, cerebrovascular disease, PAD, or diabetes with symptomatic CHD, on effective statin-based LDL-lowering therapy

n_randomized.quote: we randomly assigned 25,673 adults with vascular disease to receive 2 g of extended-release niacin and 40 mg of laropiprant or a matching placebo daily.
n_randomized.note: 12,838 niacin-laropiprant vs 12,835 placebo; 10,932 China, 14,741 Europe (UK, Scandinavia). Registry S2 enrollment 25,673 ACTUAL.

median_followup.quote: During a median follow-up period of 3.9 years
median_followup.note: 3.9 years (=46.8 months); mean 3.6 years; 46,239 vs 46,359 person-years.

primary_endpoint.value: First major vascular event: nonfatal MI, coronary death, any stroke, or arterial (coronary or noncoronary) revascularization
primary_endpoint.quote: The primary outcome was the first major vascular event (nonfatal myocardial infarction, death from coronary causes, stroke, or arterial revascularization).

inclusion_key_criteria.value: Age 50-80 with prior MI, cerebrovascular disease, PAD, or diabetes with symptomatic CHD; NO lipid entry criteria; pre-randomization run-in on simvastatin 40 mg (+ ezetimibe 10 mg if total cholesterol >=135 mg/dL) then active ERN/LRPT run-in to exclude intolerant patients
inclusion_key_criteria.quote: Men and women 50 to 80 years of age were eligible if they had a history of myocardial infarction, cerebrovascular disease, peripheral arterial disease, or diabetes mellitus with evidence of symptomatic coronary disease. There were no entry criteria regarding lipid levels.
inclusion_key_criteria.note: Active run-in excluded 33.1% of those entering ERN/LRPT phase (S6), enriching for niacin-tolerant patients.

planned_events.quote: we estimated that with more than 3400 major vascular events, the study would have more than 80% power to detect a proportional reduction in risk of 10%, at a significance level of less than 0.05
planned_events.note: Revised design after run-in lipid data showed smaller-than-anticipated lipid differences; sample increased from 20,000 to 25,000. Observed events 3,454 (1,696 + 1,758).

assumed_rrr.quote: the study would have more than 80% power to detect a proportional reduction in risk of 10%
assumed_rrr.note: Original design assumed 15% RRR (>95% power, 20,000 participants). S6: lipid differences 'might translate into a 10–15% reduction in vascular events'.

power.quote: the study would have more than 80% power to detect a proportional reduction in risk of 10%
power.note: Stated as 'more than 80%'. Original: 'more than 95% power to detect a proportional reduction in risk of 15%'.

alpha.quote: at a significance level of less than 0.05
alpha.note: Log-rank analyses with two-sided significance test.

stopped_early.note: Registry status COMPLETED (primary completion 2012-10). Ran to scheduled end of treatment period; not stopped early. Table field value only (no prose quote).

baseline.quote: with an average LDL cholesterol level of 63 mg per deciliter (1.64 mmol per liter, as measured in the central laboratory)
baseline.note: On standardized simvastatin 40 mg +/- ezetimibe, before ERN/LRPT run-in. Lower in China (1.51 mmol/L) than Europe (1.74 mmol/L) (S6 Table 3). Very low LDL-C background.

baseline.quote: and an average HDL cholesterol level of 44 mg per deciliter (1.14 mmol per liter)
baseline.note: Not selected for low HDL-C (no lipid entry criteria).

baseline.quote: HDL-C was 1.14 (0.29) mmol/L and triglycerides were 1.43 (0.84) mmol/L
baseline.note: Mean (~127 mg/dL). 64.3% fasted >8 h at this visit.
Mean, on background LDL-lowering therapy before ERN/LRPT run-in.
NOT FOUND for whole trial population; Lp(a) measured in a 3,978-participant UK/China subset (S7).
NOT FOUND (could be derived as total cholesterol 3.32 minus HDL-C 1.14 = ~2.18 mmol/L from S6, not reported directly).

biomarker_effects.method: central laboratory (assay details in Supplementary Appendix, not read; direct vs calculated NOT FOUND)
biomarker_effects.quote: assignment to treatment with niacin–laropiprant was associated with an average reduction in the LDL cholesterol level of 10 mg per deciliter (0.25 mmol per liter, as measured in the central laboratory)
biomarker_effects.note: -10 mg/dL. Diluted by 25.4% vs 16.6% discontinuation. Authors: expected 5-6% MVE reduction from this LDL-C difference.

biomarker_effects.quote: an average increase in the HDL cholesterol level of 6 mg per deciliter (0.16 mmol per liter)
and an average reduction in the triglyceride level of 33 mg per deciliter
biomarker_effects.note: -33 mg/dL (0.37 mmol/L, per continuation of same sentence: '(0.37 mmol per liter), as compared with assignment to placebo').

biomarker_effects.method: not read in detail (subset of 3,978 UK/China participants; apo(a) isoform by agarose gel electrophoresis)
biomarker_effects.quote: Allocation to niacin–laropiprant reduced mean Lp(a) by 12 (SE, 1) nmol/L overall and 34 (6) nmol/L in the top quintile by baseline Lp(a) level (Lp[a] ≥128 nmol/L). The mean proportional reduction in Lp(a) with niacin–laropiprant was 31%
biomarker_effects.note: Proportional reduction strongly dependent on apo(a) isoform size (only 18% in top Lp(a) quintile). NEJM (S1) only states reductions in Lp(a) (Table S4, not read).
NOT FOUND in main text (S1 points to Supplementary Table S4, not accessed).

biomarker_effects.timepoint: ~8-week active run-in (ERN/LRPT 1 g x4 wk then 2 g x4 wk)
biomarker_effects.quote: Following the addition of run-in treatment with ERN/LRPT, there were reductions in LDL-C of 0.34 (SE 0.003) mmol/L, apoB of 0.10 (0.001) g/L, and triglycerides of 0.26 (0.004) mmol/L, and increases in HDL-C of 0.18 (0.001) mmol/L and apoA1 of 0.06 (0.001) g/L
biomarker_effects.note: Uncontrolled within-person run-in change (not placebo-adjusted); on simvastatin background. Table 3 % changes: LDL-C −19.9, apoB −13.5, HDL-C +16.9, apoA1 +4.8, TG mean −12.0 (median −19.5). Published after readout (2013-02-26).
Uncontrolled run-in change; randomized-phase apoB difference would be smaller given non-adherence (by analogy to LDL-C 0.34 run-in vs 0.25 randomized).

biomarker_effects.quote: ERN/LRPT 2 g produced significant changes vs. placebo in LDL-C (-18.4%), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C; 20.0%), LDL-C:HDL-C (-31.2%), non-HDL-C (-19.8%), triglycerides (TG; -25.8%), apolipoprotein (Apo) B (-18.8%), Apo A-I (6.9%), total cholesterol (TC; -8.5%), TC:HDL-C (-23.1%) and lipoprotein(a) (-20.8%) across weeks 12-24.
biomarker_effects.note: PRE-READOUT (2008) placebo-controlled lipid trial of ERN/LRPT 2 g in dyslipidaemic patients largely NOT on statin background; same quote supports the next five entries.

hr.quote: (1696 participants with events [13.2%] and 1758 participants with events [13.7%], respectively; rate ratio, 0.96; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.90 to 1.03; P = 0.29)
hr.location: Results, Effects on Major Vascular Events
hr.note: Log-rank average rate ratio, not Cox HR. Same values in Merck ACC release (S5). Registry S2 posts counts only, no ratio.

safety_signals.quote: highly significant excess of participants with fatal or nonfatal serious adverse events (7137 [55.6%] vs. 6762 [52.7%], P<0.001)
safety_signals.location: Results, Effects on Other Adverse Events
safety_signals.note: Registry S2 SAE counts match (7137/12838 vs 6762/12835). Merck 2012-12-20 release (S3) disclosed 'a statistically significant increase in the incidence of some types of non-fatal serious adverse events' at readout.

safety_signals.signal: serious disturbance of diabetes control (patients with diabetes)
safety_signals.quote: associated with a 55% proportional increase in disturbances in diabetes control that were considered to be serious, most of which led to hospitalization (11.1% vs. 7.5%, P<0.001)
associated with a 32% proportional increase in the diagnosis of diabetes (5.7% vs. 4.3%, P<0.001)
The excess of infections with niacin–laropiprant versus placebo (8.0% vs. 6.6%, P<0.001) was distributed across a range of sites and types of infection
safety_signals.note: Unexpected. AIM-HIGH (niacin alone) also showed 8.1% vs 5.8%, P=0.008, suggesting niacin rather than laropiprant.

safety_signals.quote: (2.5% vs. 1.9%, P<0.001) was distributed across a number of sites (and included gastrointestinal bleeding and intracranial hemorrhage)
safety_signals.note: Unexpected. Clin Ther 2019 (S8): HR 1.38 (1.17-1.63). Hemorrhagic stroke 0.9% vs 0.7%, RR 1.28 (0.97-1.69).

safety_signals.quote: (4.8% vs. 3.8%, P<0.001) included bleeding and peptic ulceration
allocation to ERN/LRPT increased the risk of definite myopathy [75 (0.16%/year) vs. 17 (0.04%/year): risk ratio 4.4; 95% CI 2.6–7.5; P < 0.0001]
safety_signals.note: Mostly in China (RR 5.2 vs 1.5 Europe). S1: musculoskeletal SAEs 3.7% vs 3.0%. DMC flagged myopathy in China during 2009 and the prescribing information was updated (pre-readout public signal).

safety_signals.quote: (0.7% vs. 0.4%, P = 0.003) — mostly rashes and skin ulcerations
nonsignificant 9% proportional increase in the incidence of death from any cause (798 participants [6.2%] and 732 participants [5.7%], respectively; rate ratio, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.99 to 1.21; P = 0.08)

genetics.finding: Mendelian randomization: HDL-raising LIPG Asn396Ser and a 14-SNP HDL-C score not associated with MI; LDL-C score strongly associated
genetics.quote: However, a 1 SD increase in HDL cholesterol due to genetic score was not associated with risk of myocardial infarction (OR 0·93, 95% CI 0·68–1·26, p=0·63).
genetics.note: PRE-readout: Lancet online 2012-05-17, ~7 months BEFORE HPS2-THRIVE readout (2012-12-20). Full text read in PMC.

genetics.finding: Heterozygous ABCA1 loss-of-function lowers HDL-C by 17 mg/dL without increasing ischemic heart disease risk
genetics.quote: Heterozygotes vs noncarriers for 4 ABCA1 mutations (P1065S, G1216V, N1800H, R2144X) had HDL cholesterol levels of 41 mg/dL (interquartile range, 31-50 mg/dL) vs 58 mg/dL (interquartile range, 46-73 mg/dL), corresponding to a reduction in HDL cholesterol of 17 mg/dL (P < .001).

genetics.finding: LPA variants raising Lp(a) associated with CAD, supporting causal Lp(a)
genetics.quote: Our findings provide support for a causal role of Lp(a) lipoprotein in coronary disease.
genetics.note: PRE-readout. Later trial analysis (S7, 2018) estimated niacin's Lp(a) reduction would yield only ~2% coronary risk reduction overall.

genetics.finding: GPR109A (HCAR2)-knockout mice retain niacin lipid efficacy; full GPR109A agonists did not reproduce niacin lipid effects in humans
genetics.effect: Lipid effects not mediated by HCAR2
genetics.quote: We conclude that the GPR109A receptor does not mediate niacin's lipid efficacy, challenging the long-standing FFA hypothesis.
genetics.note: PRE-readout (Aug 2012). Animal + human pharmacology, not human genetics. Europe PMC lists 2012-08-01.

genetics.finding: Mouse PUMA-G (Hcar2) knockout abolishes niacin anti-lipolytic and acute FFA/TG lowering
genetics.quote: In mice lacking PUMA-G, the nicotinic acid-induced decrease in free fatty acid (FFA) and triglyceride plasma levels was abrogated, indicating that PUMA-G mediates the anti-lipolytic and lipid-lowering effects of nicotinic acid in vivo.
genetics.note: Human genetic evidence on HCAR2 or PTGDR (laropiprant target) and CVD: NOT FOUND.

consensus_explanation.summary: Consensus: niacin's cardiovascular hypothesis rested largely on raising HDL-C, which is not causally protective (Mendelian randomization, ABCA1/LIPG genetics, CETP-inhibitor failures), so the only plausible benefit was via its modest apoB/LDL-C (and Lp(a)) lowering. On a background of effective statin (+/- ezetimibe) therapy with mean LDL-C already 63 mg/dL, niacin-laropiprant lowered LDL-C by only ~10 mg/dL (0.25 mmol/L) on average (diluted by ~25% discontinuation); by CTT estimates this predicts only ~5-6% fewer major vascular events, and the investigators judged the combined lipid changes compatible with ~10% at most; the observed 4% (RR 0.96, 0.90-1.03) is statistically consistent. Meanwhile niacin(-laropiprant) caused clinically important harms: excess serious diabetes complications and new diabetes, infections, bleeding, GI and musculoskeletal (myopathy, especially in Chinese patients on simvastatin) events, with a non-significant 9% rise in mortality. The trial was large, well-powered and well-executed, so the null result is accepted as a true lack of net benefit of the drug/hypothesis rather than a design artifact; laropiprant's separate contribution to harms is uncertain but AIM-HIGH (niacin alone) showed similar infection signals.

pre_readout.note: Readout = Merck press release 2012-12-20 (no numbers; numeric results first at ACC 2013-03-09). Sources with pub_date before 2012-12-20 counted as available.
available_before_readout: Registry record (first posted 2007-04-18; S2) describing primary outcome and design (content of the original version not verified).
ERN/LRPT 2 g placebo-adjusted lipid effects (largely without statin): LDL-C -18.4%, HDL-C +20.0%, non-HDL-C -19.8%, TG -25.8%, apoB -18.8%, Lp(a) -20.8% (S9; 2008-12).
AIM-HIGH stopped for futility on 2011-05-26 (S11) and published 2011-11-15: HR 1.02 (0.87-1.21) with niacin on intensive statin background (S10).

Coronary Drug Project 1975 (S19) and 15-year mortality benefit 1986 (S20); HATS 2001 (S21); ARBITER 6-HALTS 2009 (S22); Bruckert 2010 meta-analysis showing ~25-27% event reductions mostly in pre-statin trials (S23).
Genetics: ABCA1 LoF (S13; 2008), LPA variants causal for CAD (S16; 2009), Voight HDL Mendelian randomization null (S12; 2012-05-17 — YES, predates readout by ~7 months).
Target biology: HCAR2 mediates anti-lipolysis (S15; 2003) but NOT niacin's lipid efficacy (S14; Aug 2012, pre-readout).
CTT 2010 per-mmol/L LDL-C benefit (S17; 2010-11-08) — allows estimating ~5-6% expected benefit from ~0.25 mmol/L LDL-C difference.
dal-OUTCOMES: CETP inhibitor dalcetrapib raised HDL-C 31-40% with no benefit, HR 1.04 (S18; NEJM 2012-11-05; topline announced May 2012 per general knowledge, not verified here).
Myopathy excess in Chinese participants flagged by DMC in 2009 with prescribing-information update (described retrospectively in S6).
only_after_readout: Trial design details incl. power, run-in lipid changes, myopathy data (S6 EHJ 2013-02-26; note it says the data-analysis plans were posted on the study website before unblinding — not verified).
Numeric primary result RR 0.96 (0.90-1.03) (S5 ACC 2013-03-09; S1 NEJM 2014-07-17).
Randomized-phase lipid differences (LDL-C -10, HDL-C +6, TG -33 mg/dL) and serious adverse event breakdown (S1, 2014).
Lp(a) reduction 31% / 12 nmol/L (S7, 2018); detailed SAE analysis (S8, 2019).

access_summary.note: Key numbers = design (n, median follow-up, planned events, RRR, power, alpha), outcome (RR, CI low/high, p, events x2), placebo-adjusted randomized-phase biomarkers (LDL-C, HDL-C, TG, Lp(a), apoB, non-HDL-C, apoA-1). NEJM publisher page returned HTTP 403, but the published PDF is freely available in the Oxford University Research Archive (ORA) and was read in full; EHJ design paper and Lp(a) paper are free in PMC. Not found: randomized-phase apoB, non-HDL-C, apoA-1 (in NEJM Supplementary Table S4, not accessed). Outcome counts are also in the registry and the RR/CI/p in the Merck ACC press release.
